questions.q: Write the two half-reactions and the overall reaction for the electrochemical rusting of iron in acidic aqueous medium, and state the standard cell potential.
questions.a: Anode: 2Fe(s) → 2Fe²⁺(aq) + 4e⁻ (E° = –0.44 V); Cathode: O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O(l) (E° = 1.23 V); Overall: 2Fe(s) + O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) → 2Fe²⁺(aq) + 2H₂O(l); E°cell = 1.67 V. A wrong answer (e.g., writing Fe → Fe³⁺ directly, omitting H⁺, or using E°cell = 0.44 V) reveals the student has not grasped the electrochemical cell model or the need to balance electrons and use reduction potentials correctly.

questions.q: Explain why rusting does not occur in completely dry air or in deoxygenated water, using the electrochemical mechanism.
questions.a: Rusting requires both O₂ (cathodic reactant) and H₂O (medium for ion transport and source of H⁺ via CO₂ dissolution). In dry air, no electrolyte exists to complete the internal circuit; in deoxygenated water, the cathodic reaction (O₂ reduction) cannot proceed. A student who says "rusting is just Fe + O₂" misses the electrochemical cell requirement of an ionic conductor and separate redox sites.

questions.q: A student sets up an experiment: two identical iron nails, one placed in tap water, the other in boiled distilled water with a layer of oil on top. After a week, only the nail in tap water rusts. Explain the result using the corrosion cell concept.
questions.a: Tap water contains dissolved O₂ and CO₂ (giving H⁺), providing both cathodic reactant and electrolyte. Boiled distilled water lacks O₂; the oil layer prevents O₂ dissolution. Without O₂, the cathodic half-reaction cannot occur, so the corrosion cell cannot function. A wrong explanation citing "boiled water is pure" without mentioning O₂ absence shows misunderstanding of the cathodic reaction's role.

questions.q: Compare the corrosion protection mechanisms of (a) painting iron, (b) galvanizing with zinc, and (c) connecting iron to a magnesium block. Identify which method(s) use sacrificial protection.
questions.a: (a) Painting: barrier protection — physically isolates metal from H₂O/O₂. (b) Galvanizing: Zn coating acts as barrier; if scratched, Zn (E° = –0.76 V) oxidises preferentially, sacrificing itself to protect Fe (cathodic protection). (c) Mg block: sacrificial anode — Mg (E° = –2.37 V) corrodes, forcing Fe to be cathode. Methods (b) and (c) use sacrificial protection. A student who says galvanizing is only barrier protection misses the electrochemical role of Zn when coating is damaged.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Stainless steel does not corrode because it contains chromium which forms a protective oxide layer; therefore, it can be used in any environment without additional protection." Is this fully correct? Justify.
questions.a: The statement is partially correct but misleading. Cr forms a passive Cr₂O₃ layer that prevents corrosion in many environments, but in chloride-rich environments (seawater), pitting corrosion can occur where the passive layer breaks down locally, creating anodic pits. Stainless steel is not immune to all corrosion. A student who agrees fully ignores the limitation of passivity and the role of aggressive ions.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using iron nails, copper wire, magnesium ribbon, and agar-gel with phenolphthalein and potassium ferricyanide to visually demonstrate cathodic protection of iron by magnesium.
questions.a: Embed an iron nail and a magnesium ribbon in the gel, connect them externally with copper wire. At the Fe cathode, O₂ reduction produces OH⁻ turning phenolphthalein pink; at the Mg anode, Mg oxidises (no colour). In a control without Mg, the nail shows blue Prussian blue (Fe³⁺ + [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻) at anodic sites. A poor design (e.g., no external connection, or using same metal) fails to show the galvanic coupling and electron flow.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Corrosion is an ______ process where a metal deteriorates due to oxidation by environmental agents (oxygen, water, acids), forming metal oxides, hydroxides, or salts.
Fill in the blank: Observe a rusted iron gate or bridge railing — the reddish-brown flaky ______ is Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.
What is Corrosion? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Corrosion is an electrochemical process where a metal deteriorates due to oxidation by environmental agents (oxygen, water, acids), forming metal oxides, hydroxides, or salts.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Corrosion?
questions.a: Students often write the rusting reaction as simply 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃, treating it as a direct chemical oxidation.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can (1) write the balanced half-reactions and overall reaction for rusting, (2) calculate the standard cell potential for the corrosion cell using standard electrode potentials, (3) explain why water and H⁺ are essential for the electrochemical mechanism, and (4) describe three prevention methods (barrier coating, sacrificial.
